catalog_quote: In EA stress is not a major problem, as its occurrence is almost totally predictable in terms of syllable structure. As in English, a word never has more than one primary, or heavy, stress; and long vowels never occur unstressed. Remember that EA does not permit more than one long vowel in a word; in case of two long vowels (resulting from morphological suffixation), the first gets shortened and the stress shifts to the second long vowel ... Bearing the above in mind, we can state the rules for EA stress as follows: GENERAL RULE: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable; e.g. /katab/ 'he wrote,' ... /madrasa/ 'school.' EXCEPTIONS: (a) Stress falls on the last syllable if it has the structure CVCC or CVV(C); e.g. /katabt/ 'I wrote,' ... /ramuu/ 'they threw it' (m), /hinaak/ 'there.' (b) Stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable if the last three syllables have the structure: CVCVCV(C)…
sweep_summary: Egyptian (Cairene) Arabic is in the catalog as weight-sensitive on Abdel-Massih 1975. Of 13 title hits, 9 are about Cairene word stress, 3 are intonation/discourse prosody (Hellmuth 2006 x2, Hellmuth 2007, Ward & Al Bayyari 2007) and one is a general theory (Hagberg). Two were obtained open and read: Welden 1980 'Stress in Cairo Arabic' (SLS 10(2), whole volume on archive.org; IDEALS hdl 2142/9324) and Hagberg 2006 (SIL e-Book 3, via Wayback copy of the SIL PDF). Welden gives a first-hand, informant-tested rule (p. 102) that confirms every clause of the catalog's rule (penult default; final CVCC/CVV(C); LLL antepenult; final CVC light; katabítu penult) and refines it (alternating count for all-light strings, unstressed long vowels shorten, proclitics outside the domain, secondary rhythmic stress exists, p. 111); it is a better deciding source than the textbook and should replace or head the citation, with the 'weight' coding unchanged. Hagberg reproduces Hayes' 1991 Cairene rule (p. 7) second-hand, consistent with both. Aquil 2014's abstract (Crossref) states primary stress is uncontroversially on one of the last three syllables and argues secondary stress exists (refines the catalog's 'no secondary stress' note). Not obtainable from our machine: McCarthy 1979 LI (JSTOR; UMass ScholarWorks 403), Welden 1977 UT Austin diss., Guindy 1988 ZAL, Harms 1981 Linguistic Analysis, Larudee 1973 Language Sciences, Hayes 1995 (Google Books preview only), Hellmuth 2006/2007 (SOAS eprints unreachable; De Gruyter paywalled).org, IDEALS, MPI PuRe and the Wayback Machine.

new_statements.quote: A CV syllable is light, as is a word-final CVC. [...] CVC when non-final is heavy. CVV, CVVC and CVCC are always heavy. [...] Statement I: Stress does not regress beyond the ante-penult. A light syllable is not stressed in final position. Statement II: The last heavy syllable is stressed in either ultimate or penultimate position, but not in ante-penultimate position. Statement III: If no heavy syllable occurs, or if it precedes the penult, stress is placed on the penultimate syllable, except in the case of words of the following shape LLL, in which the ante-penult is stressed.

new_statements.locator: Sect. 2.1 'The Rule of Stress Placement', p. 102 (examples (5) pp. 102-103: kitáab, katábt, mádrasa, súftaha, kátab, kátabu, ?imbasátu); alternating-count generalization p. 107; secondary stress Sect. 4.2.1 p. 111. scanned lines 22015-22060 of
new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive, right-edge, three-syllable window: final syllable stressed only if superheavy (CVVC/CVCC) or CVV; otherwise a heavy penult (non-final CVC, CVV) is stressed; a heavy antepenult is never stressed (mádrasa); among all-light strings the count decides (LLL -> antepenult kátabu; LLLL -> penult katabítu, generalized as even -> penult, odd -> antepenult); final CVC counts light; unstressed long vowels shorten; proclitics are outside the stress domain; secondary rhythmic stress on alternate preceding syllables. This is the same system the catalog codes ('weight', CVV+CVC heavy, right edge) and matches every clause of Abdel-Massih's rule including the katabítu exception, so the coding stands.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Coding unchanged: kind=weight, wcls=CVV+CVC (non-final CVC heavy, word-final CVC light; CVV/CVVC/CVCC always heavy), edge=right, three-syllable window, heavy antepenult never stressed (mádrasa; 9alámi from underlying /9aalam+i/ with shortening of the unstressed long vowel), LLL -> antepenult (kátabu, ?imbasátu), LLLL -> penult (katabítu, by the morphological rule Stressed-it and, in Welden's final formulation, also by the alternating count). audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held Abdel-Massih 1975 scanned at sec. 7.5, pp. 25-26 (page images also held); locator correct. (2) Deciding source is a 1975 pedagogical textbook, but the held 1979 Reference Grammar by the same authors (p. 254) states identical rules, and Woidich 1980 (Handbuch der arabischen Dialekte, pp. 210-211), fetched sources now from the Rosetta Project scan, independently confirms the weight-driven right-edge rule (stress the last vCC / long-vowel sequence if at most one syllable follows, else the vowel immediately after it; initial stress when no heavy sequence exists; 3fs-perfect and certain plurals morphologically fixed). Coding kind=weight, edge=right, wcls=CVV+CVC (final CVC not stress-attracting, final CVCC/CVV(C) attracting) is exactly what all three say and matches the well-known generative literature. (3) Not held: Woidich 2006 and Watson 20

sources.citation: Welden, Ann (1980). Stress in Cairo Arabic. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 10(2): 99-120.
sources.quote: Statement I: Stress does not regress beyond the ante-penult. A light syllable is not stressed in final position. Statement II: The last heavy syllable is stressed in either ultimate or penultimate position, but not in ante-penultimate position. Statement III: If no heavy syllable occurs, or if it precedes the penult, stress is placed on the penultimate syllable, except in the case of words of the following shape LLL, in which the ante-penult is stressed. [...] an alternating rhythmic pattern (ARP) begins to emerge: an even number of light syllables gets penultimate stress; an odd number gets ante-penultimate stress.
sources.locator: Sect. 2.1, p. 102 (Statements I-III); p. 107 (ARP); Sect. 4.2.1, p. 111 (secondary stress). scanned: lines 22040-22060, 22740-22743, 23363
sources.note: Dedicated first-hand study (Foreign Service Institute; informant-tested). Weights: CV light, word-final CVC light, non-final CVC heavy, CVV/CVVC/CVCC heavy. Stress never beyond the antepenult; a final light syllable is never stressed; the last heavy syllable is stressed in ultimate or penultimate position but NOT in antepenultimate position (mádrasa, sufˈtaha); otherwise penult, except LLL words which take the antepenult (kátabu). Four-light-syllable verbs (katabítu) are penult-stressed (morphological 'Stressed-it' rule, Sect. 3); generalized on p. 107 as an alternating rhythmic pattern: even…

sources.citation: Hagberg, Lawrence Raymond (2006). An Autosegmental Theory of Stress. SIL e-Books 3. Dallas: SIL International (revised 1993 University of Arizona dissertation).
sources.quote: (9) Stress in Cairene Arabic: a. Stress is on the last syllable, if it is superheavy. b. Otherwise, stress is on the penult, if it is heavy. c. Otherwise, stress is on the antepenult or penult, whichever is separated by an even number of syllables from the immediately preceding heavy syllable, if there is one, or from the beginning of the word if there is none, where zero is counted as even.
sources.locator: Sect. 1.2.2, p. 7 (ex. 9), p. 8 (ex. 11, Hayes' derivation); txt lines 470-530
sources.note: General theory; uses Cairene Arabic as the type case of left-headed moraic trochees (Sect. 1.2.2 pp. 7-9, Sect. 3.1.2.1). Second-hand data (Langendoen 1968, McCarthy 1979, Halle & Vergnaud 1987) and Hayes' (1991) rule: final superheavy syllable stressed; else heavy penult; else antepenult or penult, whichever is an even number of syllables from the preceding heavy syllable (or word start). Examples katábt, sakakíin; qamálti, hadáani; martába, búxala, katabítu, kátaba. Notes disagreement on secondary stress (Hayes claims it via resistance to phrasal syncope, Kenstowicz 1980). sources.quote: There is no dispute in the literature over the place of primary stress, on one of the rightmost three syllables. However, very few studies support the presence of secondary stress (Harms, 1981; Welden, 1980), while more research suggest that secondary stress does not exist (Aljarah, 2008; De Lacy, 1998; Halle & Vergnaud, 1987; Hayes, 1995; Kenstowicz, 1994; McCarthy, 1979; Watson, 2002). Although I agree with research (Gairdner, 1926; Harms, 1981; Welden, 1980) that secondary stress exists in CA, I refute the data and analysis proposed by this research.
sources.note: Abstract (Crossref): primary stress uncontroversially on one of the rightmost three syllables; argues with OT constraints (FootBinarity, Align-Head/R, Trochaic, WSP, *Clash, *Lapse) that secondary stress exists, siding with Gairdner 1926, Harms 1981, Welden 1980 against Hayes 1995, McCarthy 1979, Watson 2002 etc., while refuting the earlier data. Refines the catalog's 'no secondary stress described' field; primary-stress coding unaffected. Full text paywalled.
